title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E526 sets up the general equation for small transverse vibrations of an elastic rod (Problem 1, §4). On the previous page Euler took the rod EF of length a with cross-section cc, measured forces by volumes of the rod's material, and set the mass per unit length S = cc. For small vibrations he put s ≈ x and treated the motion as purely transverse, so x_tt = 0 and the curvature is 1/r = -y''. He wrote the absolute elasticity as V = b c^4.

On this page:
(1) Dimensional check. V/r is a moment, and forces are measured as volumes (three lengths), so V/r carries four lengths. Hence b is a length; b c^4 is the flexural rigidity in Euler's units.
(2) Loads. There are no distributed external forces (P = Q = 0). At the end E he applies an axial force E along EF and a transverse force F along Ef, giving ∫P ds = E and ∫Q ds = F.
(3) Effective forces (d'Alembert). P' = P - (cc/2g) x_tt = P, since x_tt = 0, so ∫P' ds = E. Also Q' = Q - (cc/2g) y_tt, so ∫Q' ds = F - (cc/2g)∫ y_tt ds. The factor 2g reflects Euler's convention that acceleration = 2g × force/mass.
(4) Moment balance about the current point gives the integro-differential equation
 E y - F x + (cc/2g)∫dx∫ds y_tt = -b c^4 y''.
(5) Tension. The longitudinal tension is -E - y'∫Q' ds, which is about -E because y' is small. So with E = 0 the rod is unstressed axially.
(6) Differentiation. Differentiating once with ds constant and dividing by ds gives
 E y' - F + (cc/2g)∫y_tt ds = -b c^4 y'''.
The next page differentiates once more to reach
 E y'' + (cc/2g) y_tt = -b c^4 y''''.
This is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation with axial load: ρA y_tt = T y'' - EI y'''' with T = -E. For E = 0 it reduces to the free beam equation y_tt = -2g b cc y''''.
errors: The justification printed as 'ob (ddy/dt^2) = 0' must mean (ddx/dt^2) = 0. The transverse acceleration is not zero; the longitudinal one was set to zero on the previous page. This is either a misprint in the original or a transcription slip.

No substantive mathematical error. The signs are consistent: since tension = -E, the final equation matches the modern ρA y_tt = T y'' - EI y''''. The integration constants are absorbed by the end-load conditions at E.
Standard small-deflection approximations are made (s = x, curvature = -y'', tension ≈ -E). Rotary inertia and shear are neglected, as in all 18th-century theory.

ideas.what: Dimensional analysis showing the elastic constant b is a length when forces are measured by volumes of the material
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this kind of argument is common in his elasticity papers)
ideas.where_published: E526 itself; similar remarks in Euler's other elastic-rod papers of the 1770s

ideas.what: Derivation of the transverse vibration equation of a rod via moment balance with d'Alembert inertial forces, including an axial end load
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli beam equation with axial tension or compression (string–beam equation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1735–1744) for the free beam; Euler for the version with axial load (discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies, 1960)
ideas.where_published: E526 (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1779, publ. 1782); related material in E443 and earlier rod papers

ideas.what: Identification of the axial tension as -E for small deflections, so that E = 0 gives a tension-free rod

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard and well-documented derivation of the beam equation with axial load in a paper Truesdell analysed in detail. There is nothing unfinished or uncredited on this page.
transcription_corrections: 'ob (ddy/dt^2) = 0' after P' = P should logically read (ddx/dt^2) = 0. If the print really shows ddy, it is a typographical error in the original.
In the tension formula, 'punctum y' refers to the point Y.
